turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I've just done her observations in the side room. Blood pressure is 118 over 74, pulse 98 beats a minute, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98 percent on air, and her respiratory rate is 16 breaths a minute. She's been talking the whole time.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely, thank you. Come on through, both of you. Tell me what's happened, in your own time.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh it's been rotten, doctor. We went to my cousin Priya's wedding, peach and cream flowers, very tasteful, though the DJ was stuck on Wham and I could have done without that. After the sit-down meal my tummy completely gave up.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's skipping the important bit. Prawn starter, then a chicken curry that had sat under the lamps for ages. I had the vegetable curry and I'm right as rain.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did the diarrhoea and the sickness actually start? A day would help, even a rough one.

[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): I can't give you one, that's the maddening thing. Was the wedding last Saturday, or the Saturday before? I even said to him it was since Diwali or after, and then I remembered Diwali was weeks ago, so that's rubbish. The runs started the night of the wedding or the next morning, and I honestly could not tell you which.
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I thought Saturday just gone, then I started doubting myself. I can't swear to the day either. Sorry.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll leave the start date open rather than invent one. How many times have you been opening your bowels?

[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I did try to count. Six, and then I lost the plot. Seven, eight, maybe nine today, all watery, brown, not bloody. And these cramps low down in my tummy, they come in waves. Oh, and the loos at that venue, don't get me started, there were only two for the whole marquee.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any black stool, or blood you might have missed? And have you vomited? Any fever?

[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No blood and nothing black, I'm sure of that. No fever, I don't think so. I felt a bit warm last night but I'm not today, and that might just have been their tropical heating. Vomiting, um, twice or three times, yesterday probably, and I'm still queasy now.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was three times, all yesterday, over the kitchen sink. Nothing today. She's nauseous, not actually being sick.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine, three. He was counting, I was busy. Still got the nausea though, proper queasy, and those cramps haven't let up.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone else from the wedding been poorly?

[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, quite a few. My cousin's husband texted, same thing, and Auntie Meena, and a friend of theirs in a red hat whose name has fallen out of my head. So it's not just my constitution. The hat was a bit much, if I'm honest, for a wedding.
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three others that we know of. Every one of them had the prawns.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, thinking it through out loud, this could be a viral gastroenteritis, norovirus does exactly this, or a bacterial one from the food, campylobacter or salmonella. Several people ill after the same meal makes a foodborne bug more likely than a one-off virus, but I am not going to call it definite food poisoning. I can't separate virus from bacteria on the story alone.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): I nearly had the paneer. I knew that curry looked tired. Hindsight, eh.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?

[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Imodium. The lad at the chemist said not to, he said loperamide can trap a bug inside if other people are going down with it, and to stick to fluids. I took it anyway because I had a shift I couldn't drop. Two milligram capsules, two yesterday afternoon and one this morning.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to stop the loperamide now. If this is bacterial, slowing the bowel can hang on to the germs. The treatment is fluid, not Imodium, and I'll come back to how to drink it.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I did say the same as the chemist. She nodded and took them anyway.

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I nodded and I still had to be on the desk. I'm the receptionist at the dental practice, Mr Shah's place, and you can't vanish to the loo every ten minutes when the waiting room's full of toothaches. I vanished anyway. It was embarrassing.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines? And any allergies to medicines or anything else?

[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Ramipril, five milligrams, every morning, for my blood pressure. No allergies at all. I did try to cut salt after the practice nurse said so, then the wedding buffet undid it, which is typical.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much are you managing to drink, and how's the urine?

[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Not enough. Plain water makes the nausea worse, so I've had sips of lemonade. I've weed twice today, darker than usual, and my mouth's like sandpaper, really thirsty. When I stand up I go a bit spinny. I haven't fainted, I just grab the doorframe.

[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): For what it's worth she kept a few sips of water down with me in the waiting room and she didn't vomit there. Pulse of 98 fits with being a little dry, but she was alert and chatting.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Your lips and tongue are dry. Tummy's soft, mildly tender across the lower abdomen, no guarding and no rebound, so nothing there is suggesting peritonitis. Putting that with the pulse and the poor urine, I'd call this mild dehydration, not enough to need a drip.

[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Good, because my neighbour had a drip for a tummy bug last winter, or it might have been the winter before, I lose whole years. I don't fancy a drip. She still talks about the sandwich they gave her afterwards, which is a strange thing to remember.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): No drip today. You're alert, you've kept some sips down, and the numbers aren't scary. What will sort the dehydration is proper oral rehydration, not lemonade on its own.

[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Mum swears by flat lemonade. She turned up with a bottle this morning and then we got onto the wedding cake, three tiers, and the top one was dry, which is ironic given the state of me.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Flat lemonade isn't oral rehydration solution. Please get Dioralyte or a similar sachet, one sachet in 200 mils of water, and sip it little and often, including after each loose stool. If you start vomiting every sip back, if you can barely pass urine, if you feel properly faint, or if you see blood, that's A&E, especially out of hours.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll pick the sachets up on the way home. Is she allowed to eat?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small bland things if she fancies them, toast, rice, a banana. Nothing spicy, and don't force a meal. And the Imodium stays stopped.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): My cousin said they sent a sample of his. Should you not test mine?

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not sending a stool sample today. If this hasn't clearly settled in three days, or if blood appears, then we send a culture. A result this afternoon wouldn't change the fluids and the waiting, so I won't pretend it would.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): I was rather hoping you'd just switch it off. Some tablet that stops it dead.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know the feeling. Antibiotics aren't the right move on this story, not without blood, a high fever, or a sample that says so. Most of these burn out if you replace the fluid. I'm still leaving virus versus bacteria open.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she still take the ramipril if she's dried out? Five milligrams feels like a lot when she's not drinking.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the ramipril, five milligrams each morning, as long as she's taking fluid and not fainting. If she can't keep fluid down, hold the tablet and ring the surgery. I'm not changing the dose today.

[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): It makes me cough, that one, sometimes, and it's done it for ages. Is that even related? Also I've not been abroad, before you ask, just Leeds for the wedding. My passport expired in a drawer, whole other drama.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, ramipril can give a dry cough. I'm not swapping it in the middle of a gastroenteritis. Mention it when you're next seen about your blood pressure. We haven't booked that today.

[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): So, fluids, no Imodium, wait and see. Can I work tomorrow? Mr Shah's doing implants all morning and the new girl still can't work the software. It'll be carnage without me, carnage of a different sort.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not tomorrow. Stay off until the diarrhoea is easing and you're keeping fluid down, a day or two at least. You're infectious while it's loose, so hand washing, and don't share towels. If you're worse tonight, go to A&E as I said. If it's not clearly improving in three days, book back in with me and we'll do that stool test.
[SEG0046] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll keep an eye on her tonight and I'll get the Dioralyte. Thank you.

[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. If the actual day suddenly comes back to me I'll ring, but I wouldn't hold your breath. Those peach flowers were lovely, though. Tell whoever does your waiting room they could learn from it.
